legend: CT (A,B) and MRI (C,D) show bilateral adrenal tumours (arrows) in this patient with a family history of von Hippel–Lindau syndrome. Hyperintense tumours are identified by T2-weighted MRI (C,D). E 123I-MIBG scintigraphy shows bilateral uptake in both adrenal tumours.

diagnosis: Imaging studies in a patient with paediatric-onset phaeochromocytoma with recurrent hypertension
legend: The patient initially presented with hypertension and was found to have elevated catecholamine levels. A MRI showed a heterogeneous adrenal tumour (arrow). The adrenalectomy specimen confirmed the diagnosis of phaeochromocytoma. Subsequent genetic analysis identified a pathogenic SDHB variant. B During the follow-up period, an additional functioning tumour was noted on imaging studies using 68Ga-DOTATOC PET-CT. The tumour was not in the former surgery site, and histopathological examination confirmed this lesion as a metachronous primary paraganglioma.

diagnosis: Paediatric phaeochromocytoma
legend: Conventional cytomorphology. Like in adults, conventional phaeochromocytomas in children consist of tumour cells resembling normal chromaffin cells that display basophilic to amphophilic cytoplasmic granularity. The cells here show mild nuclear pleomorphism and occasional nuclear pseudoinclusions, which can also be seen in adrenal cortical carcinomas.

diagnosis: SDH-related paediatric phaeochromocytoma
legend: Cytoplasmic eosinophilia and/or intracytoplasmic vacuoles are variably noted in SDH-related phaeochromocytomas.

diagnosis: Adrenal gland from a patient with paediatric-onset multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 with a microphaeochromocytoma arising in the background of adrenal medullary hyperplasia
legend: Arrows indicate a microtumour in the background of expanded (hyperplastic) adrenal medulla.

diagnosis: Paediatric phaeochromocytoma
legend: Gross findings. The cut surface of the adrenal gland shows a phaeochromocytoma.

diagnosis: SDH-related paraganglioma
legend: Paragangliomas associated with a pseudohypoxia pathway alteration express inhibin; this can be misleading in the adrenal, where inhibin is often thought to indicate cortical differentiation.

diagnosis: Spectrum of morphological changes in a von Hippel–Lindau syndrome–related paediatric phaeochromocytoma
legend: Trabecular or diffuse growth with large confluent nests (shown here) and/or pseudorosettes (see Fig. <<32489>>) can also occur. The illustrated case also shows comedonecrosis. These phaeochromocytomas display variable degrees of clear cell change.

diagnosis: Biomarkers of phaeochromocytomas
legend: Like in other epithelial neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs), Ki-67 (MIB1) labelling is assessed by counting ≥ 1000 tumour cells from hotspots, either by automated image analysis or in a printed image. Markers not shown here are synaptophysin and INSM1. Although synaptophysin is positive in phaeochromocytomas, it is also expressed in adrenal cortical tumours and should not be used to distinguish the two tumour types. Because expression of GATA3 and INSM1 is not specific to paraganglial NENs, it should be assessed along with other biomarkers and correlated to the clinical context.
source: Other source (Figures A, E, F: Dr. Noriko Kimura Figures B, C, D: Dr. Ozgur Mete)

diagnosis: Clear cell change in a phaeochromocytoma
legend: Clear cell change in a phaeochromocytoma should not be mistaken for an adrenal cortical neoplasm. The spectrum of clear cell change varies in phaeochromocytomas. This photomicrograph shows an example of diffuse zona fasciculata–like clear cell change in a von Hippel–Lindau syndrome–related phaeochromocytoma.

diagnosis: Clear cell change in a phaeochromocytoma
legend: This tumour was negative for SF1 (not shown) and diffusely positive for tyrosine hydroxylase (shown here), GATA3 (not shown), and chromogranin A (not shown).

diagnosis: Intratumoural sustentacular cells in paediatric phaeochromocytoma
legend: Tumours show intertumoural and intratumoural variations in sustentacular cells, ranging from a well-developed sustentacular cell network (shown here) to a reduced or disorganized sustentacular cell network. Evidence suggests that sustentacular cells are non-neoplastic in nature. S100 (shown here) and SOX10 stain sustentacular cells. The use of sustentacular cell biomarkers is not required for the diagnosis of phaeochromocytoma.

diagnosis: SDHB is a crucial molecular immunohistochemistry biomarker in the detection of SDH-related pathogenesis
legend: Normal staining is characterized by the presence of intracytoplasmic granular reactivity in the neoplastic cells as well as in the non-neoplastic elements including endothelial cells and inflammatory cells. The granularity corresponds to the mitochondrial localization of SDHB.

diagnosis: SDHB is a crucial molecular immunohistochemistry biomarker in the detection of SDH-related pathogenesis
legend: Loss of cytoplasmic granular staining is a sign of succinate dehydrogenase immunodeficiency and requires germline testing to confirm underlying pathogenic SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, and SDHAF2 variants. The presence of positive staining in endothelial cells is an obligatory endogenous control.

diagnosis: CAIX as a molecular immunohistochemistry biomarker for VHL-related pathogenesis
legend: Membranous CAIX reactivity is illustrated in a VHL-related phaeochromocytoma. Note that negative staining does not exclude the possibility of von Hippel–Lindau syndrome. However, given the high frequency of VHL-related paediatric-onset phaeochromocytomas, pathologists can use this ancillary biomarker to facilitate germline screening in patients with no family history.

diagnosis: CAIX as a molecular immunohistochemistry biomarker for VHL-related pathogenesis
legend: Note that there is no loss of SDHB immunoreactivity.

diagnosis: Pheochromocytoma
legend: The large, confluent nests of paraganglia cells are noted extending into the adjacent soft tissues. There is tumour necrosis and increased cellularity, with increased mitoses. This tumour would have a high risk stratification score.
